client: I got a rejection letter from my dream university last week, and honestly it's been really hard to shake off. I keep thinking that maybe I was never good enough to begin with, and that this just proves it. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything — like, the letter still says what it says, right?
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds genuinely heavy — and I can hear in the quietness of how you're speaking that this has really settled into you in a painful way. That thought, "I was never good enough," is actually a really important one to look at together, because a single decision from an admissions committee is telling us about *fit and competition* that day, not about your fundamental worth or capability. And you're right that talking won't change the letter — but it can help us examine whether that letter is actually the evidence you're treating it as, or whether your mind is drawing a much bigger conclusion than the facts support.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that — like, logically I get that one rejection doesn't define me. But it's not just this letter, you know? It feels like it's the latest in a long line of things that haven't worked out, and my brain keeps connecting all of them together like they're proof of something.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly but quickly, like the words are almost tumbling out under pressure — tells me this has been building for a while, and that your mind has been working overtime connecting these dots into a story about yourself. That pattern your brain is creating, linking disappointments together as "proof," is actually a really common cognitive pattern called **overgeneralization**, where we unconsciously curate only the evidence that confirms our fears and overlook the counter-evidence. I'd really like to explore that "long line of things" with you — not to dismiss them, but to look honestly at whether your brain is being a fair judge or a prosecutor who's already decided the verdict.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess that's a fair way to put it — the prosecutor thing. But here's what makes it hard: when I try to think of counter-evidence, the good stuff feels smaller somehow, like it doesn't carry the same weight as the failures. I'm not sure if that's the overgeneralization you're talking about, or if I'm just being realistic about my track record.
therapist: That soft, almost tentative way you're describing this — like you're carefully weighing each word — really reflects how genuinely uncertain and worn down you're feeling right now, and I want to validate that this isn't easy thinking to challenge. But what you're describing, where the good things feel smaller and lighter than the painful things, is actually a hallmark of a cognitive bias called **negative filtering** — your mind has essentially put a thumb on the scale, and it's not a fair weighing system. The question worth sitting with isn't "am I being realistic?" but rather "would I apply this same unequal measuring system to someone I care about, or only to myself?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That question actually kind of stops me, because no — I wouldn't do that to a friend. If my friend got rejected from their dream school, I'd probably tell them it doesn't mean they're not good enough. But when it comes to myself, it's like there's this different set of rules, and I don't fully understand why I can't just apply the same logic to my own situation.
therapist: The fact that you paused on that question — and that I can hear something almost like surprise in your voice, speaking quickly like this realization is catching you off guard — tells me this is a genuinely important moment of insight for you. What you've just identified, that double standard between how you treat a friend versus yourself, is actually one of the most powerful entry points in this kind of work, because it shows you *already have* the compassionate logic inside you — it's just not being aimed at yourself yet. The next step isn't figuring out why that gap exists before you can close it, but rather practicing the deliberate act of becoming your own friend, one thought at a time.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I like the idea of that, becoming my own friend, but I'm not sure how to actually do it in the moment when the negative thoughts are hitting hardest. Like right now, sitting here talking about it, it makes sense — but when I get that next piece of bad news or setback, I honestly don't know if I'll remember to treat myself with that same kindness. It feels like the gap between understanding something intellectually and actually living it is really wide.
therapist: The way you're speaking — with that higher, almost searching quality in your voice — tells me this feels like a very real and honest concern, not just abstract worry, and I want you to know that gap you're describing between *knowing* and *living* something is one of the most human struggles there is. What actually helps bridge that gap is having a concrete, almost mechanical prompt ready for those hard moments — something as simple as pausing and asking yourself "what would I say to my friend right now?" before your inner prosecutor gets to speak first. That's not a perfect solution, but it's a practice, and the fact that you can already access that compassionate voice in here means it exists in you — we just need to make it easier to reach when things get hard.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I want to try that, I really do, but I'm a little worried that in those moments I'll just forget to use it — like, when the anxiety hits, it kind of takes over and I'm not sure I'll have the presence of mind to stop and ask myself that question. therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now tells me this worry is very alive for you — this isn't a casual concern, it's coming from somewhere real and urgent. What you're describing, that fear of going through the motions without believing it, is actually completely normal at the start of this kind of practice — belief doesn't usually come *before* the action, it tends to grow *through* repeated action, even when it feels hollow at first. And for those moments when anxiety takes over, we can work on making the prompt even simpler and more automatic — even just one word, like "friend," written somewhere you'll see it, can be enough to interrupt the pattern before the prosecutor takes the stand.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I think you're right that it's been there for a long time — and honestly, just hearing you say that makes me feel a little less like I'm overreacting to one rejection letter. therapist: The softness in your voice, even as you're speaking about something that clearly frightens you, tells me this takes real courage to sit with — and I want to gently challenge that fear directly: even if we find areas where you've genuinely struggled or fallen short, that is not the same thing as the story your core belief is telling, which is that *you* are fundamentally inadequate. Falling short in some areas is something every human being can point to — it's information, not a verdict — and the goal of looking at that deeper story isn't to confirm your worst fears, but to finally examine whether those fears have been a fair and accurate narrator of your life. You don't have to be ready all at once; we can approach this slowly, and I'll be here to help you hold whatever we find.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
